query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys for high‐temperature applications, oxidation resistance and material integrity are governed by the alloy’s ability to form a continuous, adherent protective oxide (e.g., Cr2O3 or Al2O3). Insufficient concentration or disrupted formation of these oxides leads to enhanced outward diffusion of reactive elements (such as Mn), resulting in the formation of less protective oxides and accelerated degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory multiprincipal-element alloy with a balanced concentration of potential protective elements (e.g., Cr, Al) versus a variant with reduced content of these elements.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to high-temperature oxidation conditions in air.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at temperatures between 700 °C and 950 °C in a controlled air atmosphere over a predetermined time period, ensuring that thermal conditions are sufficient for protective oxide formation (or its failure).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, continuity, and adherence of the oxide scale (e.g. Cr2O3 or Al2O3) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, if the alloy composition favors the rapid formation of a stable and adherent oxide barrier, interdiffusion and further oxidation are minimized. In contrast, in alloys with insufficient protective element content, the lack of a continuous oxide allows for uncontrolled outward diffusion of reactive species (e.g., Mn), leading to the formation of more porous, less protective oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with optimized concentrations of protective elements will form a coherent, adherent oxide layer with reduced oxidation rates and improved mechanical integrity relative to baseline compositions deficient in these elements, which will show thicker, less protective oxide scales and accelerated degradation.
generation.baseline: A similar multiprincipal-element alloy composition with lower amounts of critical protective elements (e.g., reduced Cr/Al content) serving as a comparison for oxidation performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in the high-temperature range (approximately 700–950 °C) relevant for applications such as fusion plasma-facing components and other harsh environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical concentrations of protective elements for optimum oxide formation and the potential influence of other alloying components have uncertainties; moreover, scale adherence and defect structures at the microscopic scale may introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MPEA samples: one with a composition designed to have high levels of protective elements (e.g., sufficient Cr/Al to promote Cr2O3/Al2O3 formation) and a control set where these elements are intentionally reduced. Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation in an air furnace at, for example, 950 °C for an extended time period. Characterize the surface oxide layers using XRD and SEM, measure weight gain (oxidation kinetics), and assess mechanical integrity (e.g., via creep or tensile tests).
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification of oxide scales
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for oxide scale morphology
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) for oxidation kinetics (weight gain measurements)
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or creep tests) to assess material integrity post-oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high protective-element alloy does not exhibit a significantly more coherent and adherent protective oxide layer, lower oxidation rates, or improved mechanical integrity compared to the control alloy, then the hypothesis that protective oxide formation governs oxidation resistance in these multiprincipal-element alloys would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

The formation of V-rich oxides and subsequent evaporation is reported to be a common reason for significant deterioration of scale adherence in TiAl-based alloys [,,,,]; however, this effect is generally observed at T ≥ 700 °C. It should be noted that the decrease in the quantity and intensity of the V2O5 oxide diffraction peaks after testing of the AlNbTiVZr0.25 alloy at 700 °C can be an indication of its partial evaporation that likely activates the breakaway oxidation at this temperature.
